query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a controlled surface aluminization treatment to cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will form a thin, adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale that significantly enhances high-temperature oxygen resistance without degrading its inherent room-temperature ductility or its yield strength at 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% tensile ductility at room temperature and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.intervention: Controlled surface aluminization via pack cementation to deposit a nano-to-micrometer-thin alumina layer on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure at 1000 °C in an oxidizing (air) atmosphere for approximately 100 hours, with subsequent mechanical testing under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent alumina (Al2O3) barrier layer on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The externally applied alumina layer acts as a diffusion barrier that impedes oxygen ingress during high temperature exposure, thereby reducing internal oxidation while leaving the cast bulk microstructure—and consequently its mechanical properties—unchanged.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated HfNbTaTiZr, the aluminized alloy will exhibit significantly reduced oxidation (evidenced by lower mass gain and minimal oxygen penetration) while maintaining its 8–16% ductility and the yield strength range of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy with known poor oxygen resistance but acceptable mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected under high-temperature (around 1000 °C) oxidizing conditions and within a limited exposure duration (e.g., ~100 hours); the intervention must not alter the core cast microstructure that imparts ductility and strength.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimum thickness of the alumina layer and its long-term stability under cyclic thermal/mechanical loads require further experimental determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples from as-cast HfNbTaTiZr: one group receives the surface aluminization treatment via pack cementation; the other group remains untreated. Expose both groups to an air atmosphere at 1000 °C for 100 hours. After exposure, conduct oxidation analyses (e.g., weight gain measurements, cross-sectional oxygen profiling) and mechanical tensile tests at room temperature and at high temperature (1000 °C) under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
measurements: Oxygen penetration depth (via microscopy or spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminized samples exhibit no statistically significant reduction in oxidation (i.e., similar mass gain and oxygen penetration as untreated samples) or if there is a measurable degradation in room-temperature ductility or 1000 °C yield strength compared to the untreated baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

frame.system: The as‐cast equiatomic high-entropy alloy HfNbTaTiZr, which in its untreated state shows 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strengths of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
frame.goal: Enhance the alloy’s oxygen resistance at high temperature without degrading its useful mechanical performance (ductility and high-temperature strength).
frame.limitation: Poor oxygen resistance that prevents practical high-temperature applications.
root_cause_cues: poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use
constraints: Single intervention (i.e. one change/processing step) is allowed
Must not sacrifice the alloy's inherent room-temperature ductility or its high-temperature yield strength
Intervention must be compatible with the existing cast microstructure
frame.regime: High-temperature service conditions around 1000 °C in oxygen-containing atmospheres (for exposure durations on the order of hours to simulate prolonged use) and under mechanical loading at strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
prior_attempts: The untreated cast alloy, which exhibits reasonable mechanical properties but suffers from poor oxygen resistance; conventional alloying routes to improve oxidation resistance often degrade ductility or over-strengthen the material.
frame.hypothesis: A promising single intervention is to apply a controlled surface aluminization (pack cementation) treatment to the cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy. This process would deposit a thin, adherent alumina (Al₂O₃) scale on the exterior of the alloy. The mechanism is that the alumina layer serves as a highly stable barrier against oxygen diffusion at elevated temperatures, thereby significantly slowing oxidation. Prior evidence in high-temperature alloys suggests that aluminide coatings (or in-situ formed alumina scales) can effectively improve oxidation resistance without substantially affecting the underlying mechanical properties. The predicted outcome is that, relative to the untreated cast alloy, the aluminized sample would show markedly improved oxygen resistance during extended exposure at 1000 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere, while retaining its 8–16% room-temperature ductility and a yield strength within the 163–530 MPa range under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹. A controlled falsification experiment would involve subjecting both coated and uncoated samples to high-temperature oxidation tests under identical conditions (e.g., 1000 °C in air for a set duration, such as 100 hours) followed by mechanical testing. A lack of significant improvement in oxidation resistance or mechanical properties in the coated sample compared to the uncoated one would refute the hypothesis.

decision.trend: Early research on high-entropy alloys focused on optimizing the balance between strength and ductility through compositional tuning and processing techniques (e.g., melting, hot isostatic pressing, spark plasma sintering, and additive manufacturing). Some studies (such as PMC7513042) incorporated in‐situ ceramic phases (like Al2O3) to boost oxidation resistance, but this has typically been achieved through bulk modifications that also affect microstructure and often sacrifice ductility or require multi‐step routes. In contrast, the oxidation limitation of the as‐cast HfNbTaTiZr remains unaddressed by a single, targeted intervention.
decision.unsolved: A method to impart excellent oxygen resistance at high temperature—by forming a stable, protective oxide barrier—without altering the cast microstructure and compromising the inherent room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength has not been solved.
decision.lever: controlled surface aluminization (via pack cementation) to form a thin, adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale
decision.why: Surface aluminization builds on existing evidence that externally applied alumina layers can serve as effective oxygen diffusion barriers at high temperatures. This intervention directly targets the oxygen resistance without altering the alloy’s bulk properties, aligning with the need to preserve the cast microstructure and its mechanical performance under the relevant temperature and loading conditions.
